slides.title: economic differences between north and south

flashcards.front: How did the North and South differ economically before the Civil War?
flashcards.back: The North was industrializing and using railroads for transportation while the South was still rural and using rivers for transport. The South was also dependent on slave labor while the North had started becoming dependent on wage labor (workers getting paid money for their work/labor). The North was profiting from exporting manufactured goods and the South was profiting from an agricultural good - cotton.
subject: concept

slides.title: political differences between north and south

flashcards.front: How did the North and South differ when it came to enacting protective tarrifs?
flashcards.back: North favored the tariffs to protect their industry from foregien competition. the South opposed because a protective tariff would make the good Southerners regularly had to buy more expensive.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: Why did the South object to high protective tariffs before the Civil War?
flashcards.back: They were opposed to tariffs because the taxes on imported goods made manufactured products more expensive for Southern consumers, while primarily benefiting Northern industries.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: How did the North and South differ when it came to creating a national bank?
flashcards.back: North favored and demanded a national bank - thinking that it would help solidify currency and credit. South opposed because they didn't want most of the nations money to be in the hands of a few wealthy people.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: How did the North and South differ when it came to internal improvements?
flashcards.back: North faovored. They wanted the federal government to fund the building of railroads to expand further west. The South opposed because they didn't want to pay (in the form of taxes) for things that didn't directly benefit or help southerners.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: How did the North and South differ when it came to making western land cheaper and easier to get?
flashcards.back: The South and most western areas favored the cheapening of western land because the south wanted to expand plantation slavery (which required a lot of land) into new territories. Areas in the west favored the cheapening of the land to increase settlements in the west. The North opposed this because it would mean a lot of people permanently moving west and potentially leaving the new factories understaffed
subject: concept

slides.title: nature of union - differences between north and south

flashcards.front: How did the North and South differ when it came to the nature of the union?
flashcards.back: North felt the federal government had slightly more power over the states and the South felt that the individual state governments had slightly more power to decide for themselves how to operate. Both sides felt they had constitutional evidence to support their claims as to who had the final say.
subject: concept

slides.title: slavery - differences between north and south

flashcards.front: How did the North and South differ when it came to slavery?
flashcards.back: Essentially, the North and South argued over the expansion of slavery (not necessarily the banning of slavery). The North opposed the expansion of slavery because it wanted to promote and support wage labor. The South felt the plantation slave system was working well for them economically so they wanted to see slavery allowed in future territories and states.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: Why did California's request to be admitted into the Union cause a problem?
flashcards.back: It caused a problem because the Missouri Compromise of 1820 set a line that determined whether or not slavery would be allowed in new territories and states and California was mostly south of that line. The South felt the law required it to allow slavery and opposed their admittance as a free state. The North favored and supported California being allowed into the Union as a free state.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: What were the main points in the Compromise of 1850?
flashcards.back: Territory gained by the U.S. in its conflict with Mexico would be given popular soveignty to decide on allowing slavery or not to please the north and stricter terms were put on the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 to please the South

flashcards.back: The south was satisfied with the compromise and the stricter Fugitive Slave Act terms because they had felt for a long time that the North was blatantly ignoring the Fugitive Slave Act by aiding escaped slaves in their journey to freedom. The stricter terms made it a federal crime to help a fugitive slave escape but it also gave incentives for people to turn fugitives into the authorities so the South felt the resistance to the law in the North would stop.

flashcards.front: How did the North respond to the new terms of the Fugitive Slave Act created in the Compromise of 1850?
flashcards.back: The stricter terms of the Fugitive Slave Act angered the Northerers. Resistance to the law grew in the North. Many northerners began joining volunteer groups to help enslaved people escape to freedom and some northern states passed personal liberty laws.

flashcards.front: What were the elements of the Compromise of 1850?
flashcards.back: The Compromise admitted California as a free state, abolished the slave trade (but not slavery itself) in Washington D.C., and established a more strict Fugitive Slave Act.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: How did the Compromise of 1850 contribute to the sectional crisis?
flashcards.back: While it temporarily eased tensions, it also introduced the strict Fugitive Slave Act, which outraged Northerners and strengthened the abolitionist movement, ultimately deepening the divide between North and South.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: In 1857, what act of Congress was declared unconstitutional by the United States Supreme Court in the Dred Scott decision?
flashcards.back: The Missouri Compromise of 1820. The Court ruled that Congress had no power to prohibit slavery in the territories.
subject: concept

event

flashcards.front: What is the significance of the Supreme Court's ruling in the Dred Scott case?
flashcards.back: The ruling declared that living in a free-state did not make a slave free, slaves were considered property under the Constitution, all African Americans, even if they were free, were not considered U.S. citizens, and most importantly; it ruled that the Missouri Compromise of 1820 was unconstitutional since slaves were considered property. By overturning the Missouri Compromise, the Supreme Court had cleared the way for the extension of slavery into new territories which the South happily cheered on.
subject: concept
law/legislation/policy
event

flashcards.front: How did Lincoln and Douglas differ in their views on slavery?
flashcards.back: Douglas supported popular sovereignty, believing local settlers should decide on slavery. Lincoln, while not advocating for immediate abolition, was strongly opposed to the expansion of slavery into new territories and argued that the nation could not endure half-slave and half-free.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: What was a significant result of the Lincoln-Douglas debates?
flashcards.back: Although Stephen A. Douglas won the Senate seat, the debates brought Abraham Lincoln into the national political spotlight and solidified his reputation as a formidable opponent of the expansion of slavery.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: What is the Freeport Doctrine and who is credited for it?
flashcards.back: Stephen A. Douglas proposed this during the Lincoln-Douglas debates. His proposal was for people living in the north to elect representatives that would not enforce slave property laws as a way of getting around the law changes made in the Dred Scott ruling
subject: law/legislation/policy
event
vocab/term

flashcards.front: What was the primary reason for the opposition of the South to the election of Abraham Lincoln in 1860?
flashcards.back: Lincoln, as a Republican, ran on a platform of preventing the expansion of slavery into the new territories. The South saw this as a direct threat to the institution of slavery and their way of life.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: Compare and contrast the Nullification Crisis of 1832 with South Carolina's secession in 1860.
flashcards.back: Both were attempts by South Carolina to assert states' rights over federal authority. However, the Nullification Crisis was about a tariff and was resolved with a compromise, while the secession crisis was about slavery and led directly to the Civil War, with Lincoln refusing to compromise on the idea of an unbreakable Union.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: What were the long-term causes of the Civil War?
flashcards.back: The fundamental economic differences between the industrial North and agricultural South, which were further exacerbated by long-standing disputes over states' rights, protective tariffs, and the extension of slavery into new territories.
subject: concept

flashcards.front: What were the immediate causes of the Civil War?
flashcards.back: The specific events that rapidly led to the outbreak of war include the election of Abraham Lincoln in 1860, South Carolina's secession, and the Confederate attack on Fort Sumter.
subject: concept
